_comment: 40 hand-written questions (spec §8), each with real ground-truth chunk_ids verified by direct lookup against the fixture-stage corpus (2026-09-12) — not by trusting the retriever being evaluated. 15 clinical (NCI PDQ), 15 research (PMC OA / PubMed), 5 spanning both, 5 genuinely unanswerable by this corpus.

questions.question: What is MGMT promoter methylation and why does it matter for glioblastoma treatment?
questions.expected_answer: MGMT promoter methylation silences a DNA repair enzyme; it is an independent prognostic factor for improved survival in newly diagnosed glioblastoma and may predict response to temozolomide chemotherapy.

questions.question: What is the standard treatment for a newly diagnosed glioblastoma per NCI PDQ?
questions.expected_answer: Standard therapy, per the EORTC/NCIC randomized trial, is surgical resection followed by radiation therapy with concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide.

questions.question: What role does radiation therapy play in treating low-grade gliomas?
questions.expected_answer: The role and timing of radiation therapy for low-grade gliomas (low-grade astrocytomas, oligodendrogliomas, mixed oligoastrocytomas) is less clear-cut than for high-grade disease.

questions.question: What role does radiation therapy play in treating high-grade gliomas?
questions.expected_answer: Radiation therapy has a major role in treating high-grade gliomas; postoperative radiation therapy has been evaluated in systematic reviews.

questions.question: What are the induction therapy options for primary CNS lymphoma?
questions.expected_answer: The International Extranodal Lymphoma Study Group evaluated multiple induction chemotherapy combinations for newly diagnosed primary CNS lymphoma.

questions.question: What are the consolidation therapy options after induction chemotherapy for primary CNS lymphoma?
questions.expected_answer: Consolidation options studied include whole-brain radiotherapy (WBRT) with or without it, and autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) with or without it, compared in randomized trials.

questions.question: How are WHO grade II oligodendrogliomas treated?
questions.expected_answer: Patients with WHO grade II oligodendrogliomas generally have better prognoses than diffuse astrocytoma patients; treatment approaches are described relative to that comparison.

questions.question: What is the general treatment approach for medulloblastoma (embryonal tumors)?
questions.expected_answer: Medulloblastoma occurs primarily in children but can occur in adults; the PDQ summary defers detailed pediatric management to the separate Childhood Medulloblastoma summary.

questions.question: What treatment options exist for ependymal tumors?
questions.expected_answer: WHO grade I ependymal tumors and grade II ependymomas (subependymomas, myxopapillary ependymomas) are often curable; treatment options are described by grade.

questions.question: How are craniopharyngiomas (sellar region tumors) treated?
questions.expected_answer: WHO grade I craniopharyngiomas are often curable; options include surgery alone if fully resectable, or debulking surgery combined with other modalities.

questions.question: What is carmustine wafer (Gliadel) localized chemotherapy used for?
questions.expected_answer: Carmustine wafers deliver high-dose chemotherapy directly to the tumor bed while avoiding systemic toxicity, since malignant glioma deaths are usually due to uncontrolled local disease.

questions.question: What antiangiogenesis therapy is approved for recurrent glioblastoma?
questions.expected_answer: The FDA granted accelerated approval to bevacizumab monotherapy for progressive glioblastoma in 2009.

questions.question: What are the treatment options for patients with one to four brain metastases?
questions.expected_answer: About 10-15% of cancer patients have a single brain metastasis; radiation therapy is the mainstay of palliation, with extent of disease guiding the approach.

questions.question: What is leptomeningeal carcinomatosis and which cancers most commonly cause it?
questions.expected_answer: Leptomeningeal carcinomatosis (LC) occurs in about 5% of cancer patients; the most common sources are breast tumors (35%), lung tumors (24%), and hematologic malignancies.

questions.question: What environmental or occupational risk factors have been considered for primary CNS tumors?
questions.expected_answer: Definitive observations are few; considered risk factors include exposure to vinyl chloride, among others.

questions.question: How does ferroptosis relate to iron metabolism in glioblastoma?
questions.expected_answer: Glioblastoma cells depend on iron for growth but evade ferroptosis via iron regulation, a targetable metabolic vulnerability; ferroptosis also releases DAMPs/ROS that reprogram tumor-associated macrophages and activate CD8+ T cells.

questions.question: What is betulinic acid and how is it derived?
questions.expected_answer: Betulinic acid is a naturally occurring compound obtainable via methanolic/ethanolic extraction from plants, chemical synthesis, or microbial biotransformation.

questions.question: Why are cerebral organoids being developed as glioblastoma models?
questions.expected_answer: Glioblastoma survival outlook has improved only marginally in forty years, creating an urgent need for better ex vivo humanoid models such as cerebral organoids.

questions.question: What mechanisms allow glioblastoma to evade the immune system?
questions.expected_answer: Glioblastoma cells use a multifactorial network of endogenous and environmental regulatory mechanisms to drive immune evasion alongside proliferation, invasion, and metastasis.

questions.question: What role might the subventricular zone play in glioblastoma malignancy?
questions.expected_answer: Neurogenic zones such as the subventricular zone might serve as a cell-of-origin site, and involvement is linked to increased infiltrative growth and perfusion on imaging.

questions.question: How much survival benefit have targeted therapies demonstrated for glioma in Phase III trials?
questions.expected_answer: The impact of targeted therapies in glioma has been modest; only radiation and chemotherapy (temozolomide, PCV) have shown significant Phase III survival benefit.

questions.question: Why has grading gliomas by histology alone been controversial?
questions.expected_answer: Histological grading has been debated for decades due to technical limitations and inter-observer variation, motivating the shift toward molecular-based grading.

questions.question: What cell types are gliomas thought to originate from?
questions.expected_answer: Gliomas are thought to develop from neural stem or progenitor cells that carry tumor-initiating genetic alterations.

questions.question: What is the general epidemiology and prognosis of glioblastoma?
questions.expected_answer: Glioblastoma is the most common malignant primary brain tumor, with poor prognosis (median survival under 2 years) and a slight male predominance.

questions.question: How might MTH1 inhibition affect glioblastoma treatment resistance?
questions.expected_answer: MTH1 was studied in adult and pediatric glioblastoma cell lines as a way to counteract resistance to anti-neoplastic treatments, which currently offer only temporary relief.

questions.question: What molecular approaches are being explored for future glioma targeted therapy?
questions.expected_answer: Gliomas are classified per the WHO fifth-edition criteria, and research is exploring molecular targeted-therapy approaches beyond current epidemiological and demographic patterns.

questions.question: What has single-cell and spatial transcriptomics revealed about glioblastoma heterogeneity?
questions.expected_answer: Glioblastoma shows substantial cellular and metabolic complexity/heterogeneity, which single-cell and spatial transcriptomic methods are being used to characterize.

questions.question: What are the leading molecular mechanisms behind glioblastoma treatment resistance?
questions.expected_answer: Despite growing understanding of mechanisms underlying treatment failure, glioblastoma standard-of-care therapy remains almost invariably associated with disease progression.

questions.question: What makes glioblastoma resistant to signalling-pathway-targeted therapies?
questions.expected_answer: Glioblastoma poses significant therapeutic-resistance challenges for both adult and pediatric patients despite advances in understanding its signalling pathways.

questions.question: What molecular subtypes have been found within IDH-mutant astrocytoma?
questions.expected_answer: Spatiotemporal multi-omics analysis of IDH-mutant astrocytoma identified four clusters, including an adipogenesis/fatty-acid-metabolism subtype and a proliferative/progenitor subtype.

questions.question: How has CNS tumor classification shifted from histology toward molecular criteria, and what does the current WHO-based approach for CNS tumors emphasize?
questions.expected_answer: NCI PDQ's classification approach incorporates morphology, cytogenetics, and molecular genetics per WHO criteria; independent research confirms that histology-alone grading has been long debated, motivating the shift toward molecular-based grading.

questions.question: Why do IDH1/IDH2 and 1p/19q genomic alterations matter for glioma diagnosis and subtyping?
questions.expected_answer: PDQ identifies BRAF, IDH1/IDH2, and 1p/19q codeletion as hallmark aberrations that aid diagnosis and prognosis in glioma subtypes; research on IDH-mutant astrocytoma further subdivides that molecular group into clinically distinct clusters.

questions.question: What is the standard of care for glioblastoma, and why does research describe outcomes as still poor despite it?
questions.expected_answer: PDQ's standard of care is surgery plus concurrent/adjuvant temozolomide and radiation; research attributes continued poor outcomes to incompletely understood mechanisms of treatment resistance.

questions.question: How is bevacizumab used clinically for glioblastoma, and how do researchers characterize the broader impact of targeted therapies on glioma survival?
questions.expected_answer: PDQ notes FDA accelerated approval of bevacizumab for progressive glioblastoma in 2009; research separately describes the overall survival impact of targeted therapies in glioma as modest compared to radiation and chemotherapy.

questions.question: How common is glioblastoma/CNS tumor disease, and what is the general prognosis?
questions.expected_answer: PDQ reports brain/CNS tumors at roughly 6.2 new cases per 100,000 people/year in the US; research on glioblastoma specifically describes median survival under 2 years.
